docs.title: Every page follows the same pattern
docs.text:
1. Use: one sentence on what the thing is for.
  2. Code: a minimal, complete example you can copy.
  3. Output: the same code, rendered live on the page in a box labelled Output.
  4. Notes: common mistakes, and a Senior note with accessibility, performance or architecture advice.
<button type="button">Save</button>
Save

Senior note

Always set type on a <button>. Inside a <form>, a button with no type defaults to type="submit" and will submit the form when someone clicks it.

About the Output boxes

Output boxes sit inside this documentation site, so they pick up a little of its base styling (font, link colour). That's intentional: it shows you how elements look inside a real styled page, not in a bare browser. For a completely unstyled view, paste the code into a blank .html file.

docs.title: Try code yourself
docs.text:
• Create test.html, paste any example, and open it in a browser.
  • Open DevTools (F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I, Cmd+Option+I on macOS). In the Elements panel, click the flex or grid badge next to an element to see its layout overlay.
  • Toggle device mode (Ctrl+Shift+M) to test responsive layouts at phone widths.

docs.title: Senior & Architect Track
docs.text:
At 0–5 years, the question is "how do I build this?" At 5–15+ years, it becomes:

  • "Can everyone use this?" → Accessibility
  • "Is it fast on a ₹8,000 Android phone on a 3G connection?" → Performance
  • "Can 50 engineers keep adding to this CSS for 5 years without it rotting?" → CSS Architecture at Scale
  • "Can I explain and defend these decisions?" → Interview Questions

docs.title: What changes as you get more senior
docs.text: Mid-level Senior Staff / Principal Scope A feature A product area Many teams / the platform CSS concern "Does it look right?" "Will it break somewhere else?" "What system makes the wrong thing hard to do?" Accessibility Adds labels and alt text Audits flows; fixes focus management Builds accessible primitives into the design system; sets CI gates Performance Optimises images Owns Core Web Vitals for a product Sets budgets; chooses rendering architecture (SSR, streaming, islands) Browser support Tests in Chrome Tests on real devices Defines the support policy using Baseline; plans feature rollouts Review Gets reviewed Reviews code Reviews designs and architecture before code exists Mentoring Pairs occasionally Mentors juniors Grows other seniors; writes the team's playbook

docs.title: The senior review checklist
docs.text:
Use this on any UI pull request:

  • Semantics: correct elements (button vs link, headings in order, lists, landmarks)?
  • Keyboard: everything reachable and operable with Tab, Enter, Space, Escape, arrows? Focus visible? Focus moved correctly on open/close?
  • Screen reader: accessible names on every control? Dynamic changes announced?
  • Responsive: works at 320px, at 200% zoom, in landscape?
  • Content resilience: long words, long names, missing images, empty states, RTL?
  • Theming: dark mode, high-contrast / forced-colours mode?
  • Motion: respects prefers-reduced-motion?
  • Performance: images sized and lazy-loaded (except LCP), no layout shift, animations on transform/opacity?
  • CSS: uses tokens, no magic numbers, low specificity, no !important, no global leaks?
  • Browser support: new features behind @supports or with an acceptable fallback?

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
About 1 in 6 people worldwide lives with a significant disability (WHO, 2023). Add temporary and situational limits (a broken arm, bright sunlight, a baby in one arm) and accessibility affects everyone. In many countries it's also a legal requirement: the European Accessibility Act has applied to most consumer digital products since June 2025, and India's Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act covers many digital services.

The standard is WCAG 2.2, level AA.

docs.title: The four principles: POUR Intermediate
docs.text: Principle Means Examples Perceivable Users can sense the content Alt text, captions, contrast, no info by colour alone Operable Users can operate the UI Keyboard access, enough time, no seizure triggers, target size Understandable Users can understand it Clear labels, predictable behaviour, helpful errors Robust Works with assistive tech Valid HTML, correct name/role/value

docs.title: The 15 checks that catch most problems Intermediate
docs.text: # Check WCAG How 1 Every image has appropriate alt (empty for decorative) 1.1.1 Inspect / axe 2 Video has captions 1.2.2 <track kind="captions"> 3 Headings form a logical outline 1.3.1 HeadingsMap extension 4 Form fields have visible labels, programmatically linked 1.3.1, 3.3.2 <label for> 5 Inputs have autocomplete tokens for personal data 1.3.5 6 Text contrast ≥ 4.5:1 (≥ 3:1 for large text) 1.4.3 DevTools colour picker 7 UI component and focus ring contrast ≥ 3:1 1.4.11 8 Works at 320px wide / 400% zoom without horizontal scroll 1.4.10 Zoom the browser 9 Text spacing can be increased without breaking 1.4.12 Text spacing bookmarklet 10 Everything works with the keyboard alone 2.1.1 Unplug the mouse 11 No keyboard traps 2.1.2 Tab through modals 12 Focus is always visible and not hidden under sticky headers 2.4.7, 2.4.11 Tab through the page 13 Targets at least 24×24 CSS px 2.5.8 14 Errors are described in text and linked to the field 3.3.1 aria-describedby 15 Custom controls expose name, role, state 4.1.2 Accessibility tree in DevTools

docs.title: Semantic HTML first Beginner
docs.text:
Native elements come with keyboard support, roles and states built in. Compare:

<!-- ❌ 1 line of HTML that needs ~20 lines of JS to become accessible -->
<div class="btn" onclick="save()">Save</div>

<!-- ✅ Accessible by default -->
<button type="button" onclick="save()">Save</button>

What the <div> version is missing: focusability (tabindex="0"), a role (role="button"), Enter and Space key handlers, disabled state, form submission behaviour, and the "button" announcement.

docs.title: Focus management Advanced
docs.text:
/* Never remove outlines without a replacement. This is a strong, accessible default: */
:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #3f51b5;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

/* Keep focused elements visible under sticky headers (WCAG 2.4.11) */
html { scroll-padding-top: 5rem; }

Rules for dynamic UI:

  • Opening a dialog: move focus into it (showModal() does this). Closing: return focus to the button that opened it (<dialog> does this too).
  • Navigating in a single-page app: move focus to the new page's <h1> (with tabindex="-1") or announce the route change.
  • Deleting an item from a list: move focus to the next item, or to the list heading.
  • Off-canvas menus: make the background inert.

docs.title: Colour and contrast Intermediate
docs.text:
<p style="color:#999;background:#fff">#999 on white: 2.8:1 ✗ fails</p>
<p style="color:#767676;background:#fff">#767676 on white: 4.5:1 ✓ passes AA</p>
<p style="color:#595959;background:#fff">#595959 on white: 7:1 ✓ passes AAA</p>

#999 on white: 2.8:1 ✗ fails

#767676 on white: 4.5:1 ✓ passes AA

#595959 on white: 7:1 ✓ passes AAA

Never use colour alone to convey meaning. A red border for an error also needs an icon and text.

docs.title: Forced colours (Windows High Contrast) Advanced
docs.text:
In forced-colours mode, the OS replaces your colours. Backgrounds and box-shadows disappear, so anything that relies on them for meaning (custom checkboxes, focus rings drawn with box-shadow) vanishes.

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .btn { border: 2px solid ButtonText; }        /* system colour keywords */
  .custom-check:checked { background: Highlight; }
}
/* Use outline (not box-shadow) for focus: outlines survive forced colours. */

docs.title: Live regions Advanced
docs.text:
Announce changes that happen without a page load:

<div aria-live="polite" id="cart-status"></div>   <!-- "2 items in cart" -->
<div role="alert">Payment failed. Check your card details.</div>  <!-- assertive -->

The live region must exist in the DOM before you change its content, or screen readers may not announce it.

docs.title: Testing toolkit Intermediate
docs.text:
Tool Catches axe DevTools / Lighthouse ~30–40% of issues automatically (contrast, missing labels, ARIA misuse) Keyboard only Focus order, traps, missing focus styles, unreachable controls Screen readers: NVDA (Windows, free), VoiceOver (macOS/iOS, built in), TalkBack (Android) Names, roles, announcements, reading order Zoom to 400% Reflow and overlap bugs DevTools → Rendering → Emulate vision deficiencies Colour-only meaning @axe-core/playwright in CI Regressions on every PR

Senior note · 🔴 Expert

Automated tools can't tell you if alt text is meaningful, if focus order is logical, or if an error message is helpful. Budget for manual testing of every critical flow (sign-up, checkout, search) with a keyboard and at least one screen reader, and include disabled users in research. Bake accessible primitives (dialog, menu, tabs, combobox) into the design system once, so product teams don't re-implement them badly.

docs.title: CSS Architecture at Scale
docs.text: CSS is easy to write and hard to maintain. Every selector is global by default, and the cascade means a change in one file can break a page you've never seen. Architecture is about making the safe thing easy.

docs.title: The problems you're solving Advanced
docs.text:
1. Global namespace: two teams both write .card.
  2. Specificity creep: someone adds #app .page .card to win; the next person adds !important.
  3. Dead code: nobody dares delete CSS because nobody knows what uses it.
  4. Inconsistency: 47 shades of grey and 23 different paddings.
  5. Ordering bugs: styles depend on which file loaded last.

docs.title: The main approaches Advanced
A layered architecture that scales Expert
docs.text:
/* main.css */
@layer reset, tokens, base, layouts, components, utilities, overrides;

@import url("reset.css")       layer(reset);
@import url("tokens.css")      layer(tokens);       /* custom properties only */
@import url("base.css")        layer(base);         /* element defaults: body, a, h1… */
@import url("layouts.css")     layer(layouts);      /* .stack, .cluster, .sidebar, .grid */
@import url("components/*.css") layer(components);  /* (bundled) */
@import url("utilities.css")   layer(utilities);    /* .visually-hidden, .text-center */
/* third-party CSS goes in 'base' or its own low layer, so your components always win */
Layer Contains Specificity Rule reset Normalisation :where() → 0 Never edited per project tokens :root { --… } — The only place raw values live base Element selectors Low No classes layouts Layout primitives One class No colours or typography components One block per component One or two classes Uses tokens only utilities Single-purpose helpers One class Allowed to override components (layer order, not !important)

docs.title: Layout primitives Advanced
docs.text:
Reusable layout classes, independent of components (from the Every Layout approach):

.stack   > * + * { margin-block-start: var(--stack-space, 1rem); }
.cluster { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: var(--cluster-space, 1rem); align-items: center; }
.center  { box-sizing: content-box; max-inline-size: var(--measure, 65ch); margin-inline: auto; padding-inline: 1rem; }
.auto-grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(var(--min, 15rem), 100%), 1fr)); gap: 1rem; }
.switcher { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; }
.switcher > * { flex-grow: 1; flex-basis: calc((40rem - 100%) * 999); }   /* row ↔ column at 40rem, no media query */

Components then focus on looks, not layout.

docs.title: Enforcing it Expert
Interview Questions (graded by level)
docs.text: Click a question to reveal a model answer. Answers are short on purpose: in an interview, lead with the core idea, then add depth if asked.

docs.title: 🟢 Beginner (0–2 years)
docs.text:
What's the difference between an element and a tag?

A tag is the markup text (<p>, </p>). An element is the whole thing: opening tag, content and closing tag, which becomes a node in the DOM.

Why do we need <!doctype html>?

It switches the browser into standards mode. Without it, browsers use "quirks mode", which emulates old browser bugs (for example, a different box model).

What is semantic HTML and why does it matter?

Using elements for their meaning (<nav>, <button>, <article>) instead of generic <div>s. It gives accessibility (roles, keyboard support), SEO and maintainability for free.

<button> vs <a>?

Links navigate (change the URL). Buttons perform actions (submit, open, toggle). Using the wrong one breaks keyboard and screen reader expectations.

Block vs inline vs inline-block?

Block: new line, full width, respects width/height. Inline: flows in text, ignores width/height and vertical margins. Inline-block: flows in text but respects width/height/margins.

Explain the box model.

Content → padding → border → margin. With the default box-sizing: content-box, width sets the content only; with border-box, width includes padding and border, which is why every reset uses border-box.

How do you centre a div?

display: grid; place-items: center on the parent. Or flexbox with justify-content: center; align-items: center. For horizontal centring of a block with a width: margin-inline: auto.

rem vs em vs px?

px is fixed. em is relative to the element's own font size (compounds when nested). rem is relative to the root font size and respects the user's browser setting. Use rem for font sizes and most spacing.

What does the viewport meta tag do?

width=device-width, initial-scale=1 tells mobile browsers to use the real device width. Without it, they lay out at ~980px and zoom out, so media queries don't work as expected.

What's the difference between display: none and visibility: hidden?

display: none removes the element from layout and the accessibility tree. visibility: hidden hides it but keeps its space.

docs.title: 🟡 Intermediate (2–5 years)
docs.text:
Explain specificity. Which wins: #nav a or .menu .item a:hover?

Specificity is (IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, types). #nav a = (1,0,1). .menu .item a:hover = (0,3,1). IDs are compared first, so #nav a wins.

Flexbox vs Grid: when do you use each?

Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts where content size drives layout (navbars, toolbars, button groups). Grid for two-dimensional layouts where you define tracks and place items (page layouts, card grids, dashboards). They're often nested.

Why won't my z-index: 9999 go on top?

z-index only competes within the same stacking context. If an ancestor creates a stacking context (via opacity < 1, transform, filter, position + z-index, isolation…) that sits below another, nothing inside it can escape. Fix the ancestor's stacking, or use the top layer (<dialog>, popover).

What is margin collapse?

Adjacent vertical margins of block elements in normal flow merge into the larger one. It doesn't happen in flex/grid containers, or when padding, a border or a new BFC separates them.

What's the difference between auto-fill and auto-fit?

Both create as many tracks as fit. With few items, auto-fill keeps the empty tracks; auto-fit collapses them so items stretch to fill the row.

How does position: sticky work, and why does it sometimes fail?

It's relative until the element hits its offset (top: 0) within its nearest scrolling ancestor, then it sticks. It fails when there's no offset, when an ancestor has overflow: hidden/auto, or when the parent isn't taller than the sticky element (common in stretched flex/grid items: add align-self: start).

How do you implement dark mode?

Define colours as custom properties, switch them under @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark), set color-scheme: light dark so native controls adapt, and add a [data-theme] override for a manual toggle stored in localStorage. light-dark() shortens this.

How do responsive images work?

srcset with width descriptors lists candidate files, sizes tells the browser how wide the image will display, and the browser picks the best file for the screen's width and pixel density. <picture> with <source media> is for art direction (different crops), and <source type> for format fallbacks (AVIF → WebP → JPEG).

defer vs async?

Both download in parallel without blocking parsing. defer executes in order after parsing finishes. async executes as soon as it downloads, in any order. Modules are deferred by default.

Which CSS properties are cheap to animate, and why?

transform and opacity: the compositor handles them on the GPU without re-running layout or paint. Animating width, height, top or margin triggers layout on every frame.

docs.title: 🟠 Advanced (5–10 years)
docs.text:
Explain the full cascade order.

Origin and importance (transitions > !important user-agent > !important user > !important author > animations > normal author > user > user-agent) → context (shadow DOM) → element-attached styles → cascade layers → specificity → order of appearance.

What problem does @layer solve? How does !important interact with layers?

It orders groups of styles by intent, so a later layer wins regardless of specificity. That makes integrating resets, third-party CSS and utilities predictable without !important. Unlayered styles beat all layers. For !important declarations the layer order reverses, so earlier layers win, which lets low layers protect critical rules.

Media queries vs container queries?

Media queries respond to the viewport; container queries respond to an ancestor's size (or custom-property style). Use media queries for page-level layout and container queries for reusable components that can appear in slots of different widths.

What can :has() replace, and what are its performance considerations?

Parent and previous-sibling styling that used to need JavaScript: form-level error states, layout changes based on content, toggles without JS. Broad selectors like body:has(.x) can trigger expensive style invalidation on DOM changes; keep the anchor element close and the argument specific (.card:has(> img)).

How do you make a custom component (e.g. a dropdown) accessible?

First check for a native element (<select>, <details>, popover). If custom: correct roles and states following the ARIA Authoring Practices pattern, full keyboard support (arrows, Home/End, Escape, typeahead), focus management, an accessible name, aria-expanded/aria-controls, and testing with real screen readers.

How do you diagnose and fix a poor CLS score?

Find the shifting elements (DevTools Performance → Layout Shifts, or the web-vitals attribution build). Typical fixes: width/height or aspect-ratio on media, reserved space for ads and embeds, font metric overrides or font-display: optional, not inserting content above existing content, and animating with transform instead of layout properties.

What creates a containing block for position: fixed?

Normally the viewport. But an ancestor with transform, perspective, filter, backdrop-filter, contain: paint/layout, or will-change naming one of these becomes the containing block, so the "fixed" element scrolls with it.

How would you build a fully accessible modal today?

<dialog> + showModal(): it gives you the top layer, inert background, Escape to close, and focus moved inside and returned on close. Add aria-labelledby to its heading, style ::backdrop, lock page scroll with html:has(dialog[open]) { overflow: hidden }, and use @starting-style for the entry animation.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert (10–15+ years)
docs.text:
How would you structure CSS for a 50-engineer product with a shared design system?

Tokens as the single source of truth (generated for web, iOS, Android and Figma). A cascade-layer architecture (reset, tokens, base, layouts, components, utilities). Scoped component styles (CSS Modules, @scope, or zero-runtime CSS-in-JS). Accessible primitives built once in the design system. Stylelint rules for tokens, specificity and !important; visual regression and axe in CI; Storybook docs; ADRs for each major decision; and a deprecation process for old components.

How do you decide which new CSS features a team may use?

Use Baseline as the default policy ("widely available" is free to use; "newly available" with @supports fallbacks). Cross-check with your own analytics (which browsers your users actually have). Require progressive enhancement: the experience must work without the feature. Document approved features and their fallbacks in the team's guidelines, and review the list every quarter.

Utility-first CSS vs component CSS: how do you choose?

Utilities: fast iteration, guaranteed token use, no dead CSS, great for app teams owning their own UI. Component CSS: cleaner markup, better for a design system consumed by many teams and frameworks, easier to theme at the component level. Many orgs combine them: a component library styled internally, with utilities for layout glue. The deciding factors are team size and structure, how many consumers there are, and whether you need framework independence.

A page's INP is 450 ms on mid-range Android. Walk through your approach.

Measure first with RUM attribution to find the slow interactions and their phase (input delay, processing, presentation). Typical causes: long main-thread tasks from hydration or third-party scripts, heavy event handlers, huge DOM style recalculations. Fixes: break up long tasks (scheduler.yield()), defer non-critical JS, replace JS widgets with native elements, use content-visibility and containment to shrink rendering work, cut DOM size, and move work off the main thread. Verify with field data after release, not just lab data.

How do you make accessibility sustainable rather than a one-off audit?

Shift left: accessible primitives in the design system, accessibility acceptance criteria in tickets, design reviews that check focus order and contrast, automated checks in CI as a floor (not a ceiling), manual keyboard and screen-reader testing on critical flows each release, accessibility champions in each team, and including disabled users in research. Track issues as bugs with severity, not as "nice to have".

Explain the trade-offs of Shadow DOM for a cross-framework design system.

Pros: true style encapsulation, framework-agnostic custom elements, slots for composition. Cons: global styles (resets, fonts, utilities) don't reach inside; theming needs custom properties and ::part; SSR needs declarative shadow DOM; form participation needs ElementInternals; ARIA ID references can't cross shadow boundaries yet (reference target is still being standardised). Many teams use light-DOM components with @scope or CSS Modules instead, unless they truly need to serve multiple frameworks.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Speed is a feature. Slow pages lose users and rank lower in search. Google's Core Web Vitals are the shared yardstick.

docs.title: Core Web Vitals Intermediate
docs.text:
Metric Measures Good HTML/CSS levers LCP: Largest Contentful Paint When the main content (hero image or headline) appears ≤ 2.5 s Preload / fetchpriority="high" on the hero image, never lazy-load it, inline critical CSS, fast fonts INP: Interaction to Next Paint How quickly the page responds to taps and clicks ≤ 200 ms Less JS; native elements (dialog, details, popover) instead of heavy widgets; content-visibility to shrink rendering work CLS: Cumulative Layout Shift How much things jump around while loading ≤ 0.1 width/height on images and iframes, aspect-ratio, reserved space for ads/embeds, font-display + metric overrides

Measured at the 75th percentile of real users. Check yours with PageSpeed Insights (field data) and DevTools Performance panel (lab data).

docs.title: The critical rendering path Advanced
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    HTML --> DOM
    CSS --> CSSOM
    DOM --> RT[Render tree]
    CSSOM --> RT
    RT --> Layout --> Paint --> Composite
    JS -. "blocks parsing<br/>(unless defer/async/module)" .-> DOM
  • CSS is render-blocking: the browser won't paint until it has the CSS. Keep the critical CSS small; split the rest.
  • Classic <script> is parser-blocking. Use defer or type="module".
  • Every change to layout properties (width, top, font-size) re-runs Layout → Paint → Composite. Changes to transform and opacity only re-run Composite.

docs.title: HTML wins Intermediate
docs.text:
<!-- Hero image: high priority, no lazy loading, explicit size -->
<img src="hero.avif" alt="…" width="1600" height="900" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async">

<!-- Below-the-fold images: lazy -->
<img src="card.avif" alt="…" width="400" height="300" loading="lazy" decoding="async">

<!-- Iframes (maps, videos): lazy -->
<iframe src="…" title="…" loading="lazy" width="560" height="315"></iframe>

<!-- Early connections to critical third-party origins -->
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://cdn.example.com" crossorigin>

<!-- Preload the main web font -->
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

<!-- Speculative prefetch/prerender of likely next pages (Chromium) -->
<script type="speculationrules">
  { "prerender": [{ "where": { "href_matches": "/product/*" }, "eagerness": "moderate" }] }
</script>

docs.title: CSS wins Advanced
docs.text:
/* Skip rendering work for off-screen sections until they're near the viewport */
.section {
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: auto 800px;   /* placeholder height so the scrollbar is stable */
}

/* Isolate a widget so its changes don't trigger page-wide layout */
.widget { contain: layout paint; }

/* Animate only compositor-friendly properties */
.card { transition: transform .2s, opacity .2s; }

/* Reserve space for late-loading content */
.ad-slot { min-height: 250px; }
.embed { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; }
  • Avoid @import in production CSS: each import is a sequential request.
  • Remove unused CSS: the DevTools Coverage tab shows how much of each file is used.
  • Avoid huge DOMs: over ~1,500 nodes slows style recalculation and layout. Virtualise long lists.
  • Fonts: WOFF2 only, subset to the characters you need, variable fonts instead of 6 separate weights, font-display: optional or swap with metric overrides.

docs.title: Images Intermediate
docs.text: Do Why AVIF → WebP → JPEG via <picture> AVIF is often ~50% smaller than JPEG srcset + sizes Phones don't download desktop-sized images width + height attributes Prevents CLS loading="lazy" below the fold Saves bandwidth SVG for icons and logos Tiny and sharp at any size <video> instead of GIF 5–20× smaller

docs.title: Budgets Expert
docs.text:
Set limits, then enforce them in CI (Lighthouse CI, size-limit, bundlewatch):

Resource Example budget (mid-range mobile) Critical CSS (inlined) ≤ 14 KB compressed (fits in the first TCP round trip) Total CSS ≤ 60 KB compressed JS on initial load ≤ 150 KB compressed Hero image ≤ 150 KB Web fonts ≤ 2 files, ≤ 100 KB total LCP (lab, Moto G Power, slow 4G) ≤ 2.5 s

Senior note · 🔴 Expert

The biggest performance wins are usually architectural, not micro-optimisations: ship less JavaScript (server-render, islands, native HTML features), cache aggressively at the CDN with immutable hashed assets, and measure real users (RUM via the web-vitals library) rather than trusting a fast laptop. Make performance visible: a dashboard of p75 LCP/INP/CLS per page type, reviewed every sprint.

docs.title: Learning Roadmap: 0 to 15+ Years
docs.text:
Frontend skill doesn't grow in a straight line. It grows in layers: first you make things appear, then you make them work everywhere, then you make them fast and accessible, then you make it possible for fifty other people to do the same without breaking each other's work.

flowchart LR
    A["🟢 Beginner<br/>0–2 yrs<br/>Make it appear"] --> B["🟡 Intermediate<br/>2–5 yrs<br/>Make it work everywhere"]
    B --> C["🟠 Advanced<br/>5–10 yrs<br/>Make it fast, accessible, robust"]
    C --> D["🔴 Expert<br/>10–15+ yrs<br/>Make it scale across teams"]

docs.title: 🟢 Beginner (0–2 years): make it appear
docs.text:
You can: build a static page from a design, using semantic HTML and a single stylesheet.

  • Write a valid HTML document from memory (<!doctype html>, lang, charset, viewport meta).
  • Choose the right element: <button> vs <a>, <ul> vs <ol>, <section> vs <div>.
  • Explain the box model and why box-sizing: border-box is everyone's default.
  • Use class selectors, descendant and child combinators, :hover and :focus-visible.
  • Use rem for font sizes and know why px font sizes hurt accessibility.
  • Build a navbar and a card row with Flexbox.
  • Build a responsive card grid with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(…)).
  • Write one mobile-first media query.
  • Build an accessible form: every input has a <label>.

Done looks like: you can rebuild the pricing table and sticky header recipes without looking.

docs.title: 🟡 Intermediate (2–5 years): make it work everywhere
docs.text:
You can: ship production UI that works on every screen size and browser your users have, and debug layout bugs quickly.

  • Explain the cascade in order: origin & importance → context → layers → specificity → order.
  • Debug stacking-context bugs (why z-index: 9999 "doesn't work").
  • Know when to pick Flexbox vs Grid, and use grid-template-areas.
  • Use custom properties for theming, and implement dark mode with prefers-color-scheme.
  • Serve responsive images with srcset/sizes and <picture>.
  • Use <dialog>, <details>, and the popover API instead of hand-rolled JS widgets.
  • Animate only transform and opacity, and honour prefers-reduced-motion.
  • Use the DevTools Layout, Computed and Rendering panels fluently.

Done looks like: you can rebuild the whole Layout Gallery from screenshots.

docs.title: 🟠 Advanced (5–10 years): make it fast, accessible and robust
docs.text:
You can: own the quality of a product's UI: performance budgets, WCAG compliance and resilient CSS.

  • Meet WCAG 2.2 AA: contrast, focus order, focus visibility, target size, reduced motion.
  • Know the first rule of ARIA (don't use ARIA if a native element does the job) and when ARIA is necessary.
  • Diagnose LCP, INP and CLS problems and fix them with HTML/CSS levers (fetchpriority, width/height, content-visibility, font loading).
  • Use container queries to build components that adapt to their slot, not the viewport.
  • Use @layer to make third-party and utility CSS predictable.
  • Use :has() to replace JS-driven state classes.
  • Write progressive enhancement: wrap newer features in @supports with a working fallback.

Done looks like: you can audit an existing page and produce a prioritised list of accessibility and performance fixes.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert (10–15+ years): make it scale across teams
docs.text:
You can: set the frontend direction for an organisation. Your decisions let dozens of engineers ship consistent UI without stepping on each other.

  • Design a token system (colour, space, type, radius, motion) and its naming.
  • Choose and justify a CSS architecture (utility-first, CSS Modules, @layer + BEM, CSS-in-JS) for a given team and product.
  • Set up linting, visual regression testing and accessibility checks in CI.
  • Plan browser support using Baseline, and roll out new CSS features safely.
  • Review designs for feasibility and accessibility before a line of code is written.
  • Mentor: explain any concept on this site to a beginner in two minutes.

Done looks like: you can write the CSS Architecture page for your own company, and other teams adopt it.

docs.title: Time budget
docs.text: Level Hours/week Focus split 🟢 8–10 40% HTML, 40% CSS, 20% layout 🟡 4–6 50% layout & responsive, 30% modern CSS, 20% DevTools 🟠 3–4 40% accessibility, 40% performance, 20% modern CSS 🔴 2–3 Architecture, standards tracking, mentoring

Dense, scannable references for when you already know the concept and just need the syntax. Each sheet links back to the full chapter for explanations.

  • Flexbox

    60 live mini-diagrams: every container and item property value, everyday recipes, property table, gotchas.

  • Grid

    50+ live mini-diagrams: columns, rows, auto-fit/auto-fill, placement, named areas, alignment, layout recipes, gotchas.

docs.title: Cascade order (who wins)
docs.text:
1. Origin & importance: transitions → !important (user-agent > user > author) → animations → normal author → user → user-agent
  2. Context: outer (light DOM) vs shadow DOM
  3. Inline style=""
  4. Cascade layers: later @layer wins (reversed for !important); unlayered beats all layers
  5. Specificity: (IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, types/pseudo-elements)
  6. Order: last declared wins

docs.title: Modern reset (copy-paste)
docs.text:
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
* { margin: 0; }
html { color-scheme: light dark; -webkit-text-size-adjust: none; text-size-adjust: none; }
body { min-block-size: 100dvh; line-height: 1.5; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
img, picture, video, canvas, svg { display: block; max-inline-size: 100%; height: auto; }
input, button, textarea, select { font: inherit; }
p, h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6 { overflow-wrap: break-word; }
h1, h2, h3 { text-wrap: balance; }
p { text-wrap: pretty; }
:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid; outline-offset: 2px; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after { animation-duration: .01ms !important; transition-duration: .01ms !important; scroll-behavior: auto !important; }
}

docs.title: What "CSS3" means Intermediate
docs.text:
timeline
    1996 : CSS1 : fonts, colours, margins
    1998 : CSS2 : positioning, z-index, media types
    2011 : CSS2.1 : the stable base everyone implemented
    2011–2017 : "CSS3" modules : rounded corners, shadows, gradients, transforms, transitions, animations, media queries, flexbox, grid
    2018–2026 : Living modules : custom properties, :is/:where/:has, nesting, @layer, container queries, subgrid, view transitions, anchor positioning

After CSS2.1, CSS was split into independent modules (Selectors, Color, Flexbox, Grid…), each with its own level number. "CSS3" is just a marketing label for that first wave. There will never be a "CSS4"; the CSS Working Group publishes yearly snapshots instead, and developers track Baseline to see what's safe to use.

Baseline

Baseline marks a web feature as:

  • Newly available: works in the latest Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari.
  • Widely available: has been newly available for 30+ months, so it's safe for almost every audience.

Throughout this playbook, newer features are labelled with their Baseline year.

docs.title: A modern starter stylesheet Beginner
docs.text:
Copy this into every new project. Every line is explained in the following chapters.

/* 1. Predictable sizing */
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }

/* 2. Remove default margins, keep sensible text */
* { margin: 0; }
html { -webkit-text-size-adjust: none; text-size-adjust: none; color-scheme: light dark; }
body {
  min-block-size: 100dvh;
  line-height: 1.5;
  font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, sans-serif;
  -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;
}

/* 3. Media is responsive by default */
img, picture, video, canvas, svg { display: block; max-inline-size: 100%; height: auto; }

/* 4. Form controls inherit fonts */
input, button, textarea, select { font: inherit; }

/* 5. Avoid text overflow and ugly line breaks */
p, h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6 { overflow-wrap: break-word; }
h1, h2, h3 { text-wrap: balance; line-height: 1.15; }
p { text-wrap: pretty; }

/* 6. Visible keyboard focus */
:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #e4572e; outline-offset: 2px; }

/* 7. Respect reduced-motion preferences */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: .01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: .01ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}

docs.title: Performance rules Advanced
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S[Style] --> L[Layout] --> P[Paint] --> C[Composite]
Animating… Triggers Cost transform, opacity (+ translate, rotate, scale, filter in many cases) Composite only ✅ Cheap: runs on the GPU compositor thread color, background, box-shadow, border-radius Paint + composite ⚠️ Moderate width, height, top, left, margin, padding, font-size Layout + paint + composite ❌ Expensive: whole page may re-layout every frame

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

  • Animate transform/opacity. To "animate height", use a grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr transition, interpolate-size: allow-keywords with height: auto, or scale.
  • will-change: transform promotes an element to its own layer. Add it just before an animation and remove it after; leaving it on hundreds of elements wastes GPU memory.
  • Keep UI transitions between 150–300ms. Entering: ease-out. Exiting: ease-in. Anything over 500ms feels sluggish for UI feedback.

docs.title: Why OKLCH? Advanced
docs.text:
In HSL, hsl(60 100% 50%) (yellow) and hsl(240 100% 50%) (blue) have the same "lightness" but look completely different in brightness. OKLCH is perceptually uniform: the same L looks equally light for every hue. That makes it ideal for generating accessible palettes: keep L fixed, rotate H.

/* Same lightness and chroma, different hues: all look equally bright */
.s1 { background: oklch(70% 0.15 30); }
.s2 { background: oklch(70% 0.15 140); }
.s3 { background: oklch(70% 0.15 250); }
.s4 { background: oklch(70% 0.15 320); }
H 30 H 140 H 250 H 320 hsl 30 hsl 140 hsl 250 hsl 320

Top row: OKLCH, consistent brightness. Bottom row: HSL with the same lightness, but the green looks much brighter than the blue.

docs.title: Others
docs.text: Unit Use % Relative to the parent (for width), or the element itself (for translate) fr Fraction of free space in a grid deg, turn, rad Angles s, ms Time dpi, dppx, x Resolution (image-set, media queries)

docs.title: Maths functions IntermediateResize the window: I scale smoothly
docs.text:
width: calc(100% - 2rem);
width: min(100%, 60rem);        /* the smaller: "max 60rem, but never overflow" */
width: max(50%, 300px);         /* the larger */
font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.8rem + 1.5vw, 2rem);  /* min, preferred, max */
padding: round(up, 13px, 4px);  /* 16px */

clamp() is the backbone of fluid design: one line instead of three media queries.

<h2 style="font-size: clamp(1.2rem, 1rem + 3vw, 3rem)">Resize the window: I scale smoothly</h2>

Other functions: abs(), sign(), mod(), rem(), pow(), sqrt(), sin(), cos(), tan(), atan2(), exp(), log(), hypot(). Trig functions are handy for circular layouts.

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

For fluid type, mix rem into the middle value (1rem + 2vw, not 4vw alone). A pure vw value doesn't grow when the user zooms, which fails WCAG 1.4.4 (Resize Text). Tools like Utopia generate a full fluid type and space scale for you.

docs.title: The basics Beginner
docs.text:
Custom properties (often called CSS variables) store a value once and reuse it everywhere.

:root {
  --brand: #e4572e;
  --radius: 12px;
  --space: 1rem;
}
.btn {
  background: var(--brand);
  border-radius: var(--radius);
  padding: calc(var(--space) / 2) var(--space);
}
.btn--ghost {
  background: transparent;
  color: var(--brand);
  border: 2px solid var(--brand);
}
Primary Ghost
  • Names start with -- and are case-sensitive.
  • Fallback: var(--accent, royalblue) uses royalblue if --accent isn't set.
  • They inherit and cascade like normal properties, and they're live: change one in JS or a media query and everything using it updates.

docs.title: Scoping: the real superpower Intermediate
docs.text:
Unlike Sass variables, custom properties can be overridden for one part of the page:

.btn { background: var(--btn-bg, #e4572e); }
.danger-zone { --btn-bg: crimson; }       /* every .btn inside turns red */
.card[data-tone="calm"] { --btn-bg: seagreen; }
Default Inside .danger-zone Inside [data-tone=calm]

docs.title: Passing values from HTML Intermediate
docs.text:
<div class="bar" style="--value: 72%"></div>

.bar { background: #eee; border-radius: 99px; height: 12px; }
.bar::after { content: ""; display: block; height: 100%; width: var(--value); background: #e4572e; border-radius: inherit; }

docs.title: Dark mode Intermediate
docs.text:
Use the system setting, and let users override it with a toggle.

:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;
  --bg: #ffffff;
  --fg: #1f2329;
  --surface: #f4f5f7;
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root { --bg: #121417; --fg: #e6e8ec; --surface: #1d2129; }
}
/* Manual override (set data-theme on <html> from JS / localStorage) */
:root[data-theme="light"] { color-scheme: light; --bg: #ffffff; --fg: #1f2329; --surface: #f4f5f7; }
:root[data-theme="dark"]  { color-scheme: dark;  --bg: #121417; --fg: #e6e8ec; --surface: #1d2129; }

body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg); }
.card { background: var(--surface); }

Shorter, with light-dark() (Baseline 2024):

:root { color-scheme: light dark; }
:root[data-theme="light"] { color-scheme: light; }
:root[data-theme="dark"]  { color-scheme: dark; }
body  { background: light-dark(#fff, #121417); color: light-dark(#1f2329, #e6e8ec); }
Dark mode Card titleColours come from variables that switch with the theme.

docs.title: Design tokens Advanced
docs.text:
Tokens are named design decisions. Organise them in tiers:

:root {
  /* Tier 1: primitive tokens (the raw palette; never used directly in components) */
  --orange-500: oklch(64% 0.19 37);
  --orange-600: oklch(56% 0.19 37);
  --gray-50: oklch(98% 0 0);
  --gray-900: oklch(22% 0.01 260);
  --space-1: .25rem; --space-2: .5rem; --space-3: 1rem; --space-4: 1.5rem; --space-5: 2rem;
  --radius-sm: 4px; --radius-md: 8px; --radius-lg: 16px;

  /* Tier 2: semantic tokens (what components use) */
  --color-bg: var(--gray-50);
  --color-text: var(--gray-900);
  --color-accent: var(--orange-500);
  --color-accent-hover: var(--orange-600);

  /* Tier 3: component tokens (optional, for highly configurable components) */
  --button-bg: var(--color-accent);
  --button-radius: var(--radius-md);
}

Dark mode or a new brand only changes tier 2; no component CSS changes.

docs.title: Typed custom properties with @property Advanced Baseline 2024
docs.text:
Normal custom properties are untyped strings, so the browser can't animate them. Register a type and it can:

@property --angle {
  syntax: "<angle>";
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 0deg;
}
.spin-border {
  background: conic-gradient(from var(--angle), #e4572e, #f3a712, #3f51b5, #e4572e);
  animation: rotate 3s linear infinite;
}
@keyframes rotate { to { --angle: 360deg; } }
Animated gradient border

docs.title: Reading and writing from JavaScript Intermediate
docs.text:
const root = document.documentElement;
getComputedStyle(root).getPropertyValue('--brand');   // " #e4572e"
root.style.setProperty('--brand', 'royalblue');

// Follow the pointer
document.addEventListener('pointermove', e => {
  root.style.setProperty('--x', e.clientX + 'px');
  root.style.setProperty('--y', e.clientY + 'px');
});

Senior note · 🔴 Expert

Source your tokens from one place (a JSON file in the W3C Design Tokens format) and generate CSS, iOS, Android and Figma outputs with Style Dictionary or Terrazzo. Changing a token on the root invalidates style for the whole document. That's fine for theme switches, but avoid updating root-level variables on every pointermove on large pages; set them on the smallest element that needs them.

docs.title: Backgrounds, Borders & Effects
docs.text: These are the features most people mean by "CSS3": the things that used to need images and Photoshop.

docs.title: border-radius Beginner
docs.text:
.r1 { border-radius: 8px; }
.r2 { border-radius: 50%; }              /* circle (on a square) */
.r3 { border-radius: 999px; }            /* pill */
.r4 { border-radius: 24px 0; }           /* top-left+bottom-right / others */
.r5 { border-radius: 60% 40% 30% 70% / 60% 30% 70% 40%; }  /* blob */

New in 2025 (Chromium): corner-shape: squircle | bevel | notch | scoop changes the shape of rounded corners.

docs.title: Borders and outlines Beginner
docs.text:
border: 2px solid #e4572e;
border-style: dotted | dashed | double | groove | ridge | inset | outset;
border-inline-start: 4px solid royalblue;    /* left in LTR */
outline: 2px dashed royalblue;               /* doesn't take space */
outline-offset: 4px;
solid dashed dotted double inline-start outline + offset

docs.title: box-shadow Beginner
docs.text:
Syntax: offset-x offset-y blur spread color, plus optional inset. Comma-separate several shadows.

.s1 { box-shadow: 0 1px 3px rgb(0 0 0 / .12), 0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / .24); } /* small */
.s2 { box-shadow: 0 10px 30px -5px rgb(0 0 0 / .25); }                        /* large, soft */
.s3 { box-shadow: inset 0 2px 6px rgb(0 0 0 / .3); }                          /* inset */
.s4 { box-shadow: 0 0 0 4px #e4572e; }                                        /* ring (no layout shift) */
.s5 { box-shadow: 0 0 20px 4px rgb(228 87 46 / .7); }                         /* glow */

docs.title: text-shadow Beginner
docs.text:
.t1 { text-shadow: 2px 2px 0 #e4572e; }
.t2 { text-shadow: 0 0 8px #3f51b5; }
.t3 { text-shadow: 0 2px 4px rgb(0 0 0 / .5); }   /* legible text over images */

Retro

Neon

docs.title: Gradients Beginner → Intermediate
docs.text:
.g1 { background: linear-gradient(135deg, #e4572e, #f3a712); }
.g2 { background: radial-gradient(circle at 30% 30%, #fff, #3f51b5); }
.g3 { background: conic-gradient(#e4572e 0 40%, #f3a712 0 70%, #3f51b5 0); } /* pie chart */
.g4 { background: repeating-linear-gradient(45deg, #eee 0 10px, #ddd 10px 20px); } /* stripes */
.g5 { background: linear-gradient(in oklch 90deg, #e4572e, #3f51b5); }  /* smoother interpolation */

docs.title: Background properties Beginner
docs.text:
.hero {
  background-image: linear-gradient(rgb(0 0 0 / .5), rgb(0 0 0 / .5)),   /* overlay */
                    url("hero.jpg");                                      /* photo */
  background-size: cover;          /* fill, crop the excess  | contain: fit, may letterbox */
  background-position: center;
  background-repeat: no-repeat;
  background-attachment: fixed;    /* parallax-ish; disabled on iOS */
  background-clip: padding-box;
  background-origin: content-box;
  background-blend-mode: multiply;
}
Text over an image with an overlay

Multiple backgrounds stack: the first one listed is on top.

docs.title: opacity and filter Beginner
docs.text:
opacity: .5;
filter: blur(3px);
filter: grayscale(1);
filter: brightness(1.3) contrast(1.2) saturate(1.5);
filter: sepia(1);
filter: hue-rotate(90deg);
filter: invert(1);
filter: drop-shadow(0 4px 6px rgb(0 0 0 / .4));   /* follows the shape (PNG/SVG alpha) */
original blur grayscale sepia hue-rotate invert

docs.title: backdrop-filter (glassmorphism) Intermediate
docs.text:
Applies a filter to whatever is behind the element.

.glass {
  background: rgb(255 255 255 / .2);
  backdrop-filter: blur(12px) saturate(1.5);
  -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(12px) saturate(1.5);
  border: 1px solid rgb(255 255 255 / .35);
  border-radius: 16px;
}
Glass cardThe photo behind me is blurred.

docs.title: clip-path and mask Intermediate
docs.text:
.c1 { clip-path: circle(50%); }
.c2 { clip-path: polygon(50% 0, 100% 100%, 0 100%); }           /* triangle */
.c3 { clip-path: polygon(0 0, 100% 0, 100% 80%, 0 100%); }      /* slanted section edge */
.c4 { clip-path: inset(10% round 20px); }
.m1 { mask-image: linear-gradient(black 60%, transparent); }     /* fade out */

docs.title: Blend modes Advanced
docs.text:
.knockout { mix-blend-mode: multiply; }     /* blend with what's behind */
.duotone  { background-blend-mode: screen; }  /* blend background layers */
isolation: isolate;   /* limit blending to this stacking context */

docs.title: object-fit and aspect-ratio Beginner
docs.text:
.thumb {
  inline-size: 160px;
  aspect-ratio: 1;          /* square box, any image */
  object-fit: cover;        /* fill and crop | contain: fit inside | fill: stretch */
  object-position: top;
}
.video-wrap { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; }
fill (stretched) contain cover

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

filter, backdrop-filter, big blurred box-shadows and mix-blend-mode are paint-heavy. Animating them, or stacking many glass cards on a scrolling page, can drop frames on low-end Android phones. Profile with DevTools → Rendering → "Paint flashing", and prefer animating a pseudo-element's opacity over animating a shadow directly.

docs.title: The cascade Beginner → Advanced
docs.text:
When two rules set the same property on the same element, the cascade decides who wins. It checks these in order and stops at the first difference:

flowchart TD
    A["1 · Origin & importance<br/>transitions > !important user-agent > !important user > !important author > animations > author > user > user-agent"] --> B
    B["2 · Context<br/>Shadow DOM: outer vs inner styles"] --> C
    C["3 · Element-attached styles<br/>style="…" attribute"] --> D
    D["4 · Cascade layers<br/>later @layer wins (reversed for !important); unlayered beats layered"] --> E
    E["5 · Specificity<br/>(id, class, type)"] --> F
    F["6 · Order of appearance<br/>last one wins"]

For day-to-day work, the three that matter are layers → specificity → order.

<p class="note" id="intro">Which colour am I?</p>

<style>
  p        { color: green; }   /* (0,0,1) */
  .note    { color: blue; }    /* (0,1,0) */
  #intro   { color: crimson; } /* (1,0,0) wins: highest specificity */
  .note    { color: orange; }  /* same specificity as .note above; later, but still loses to #intro */
</style>

Which colour am I?

docs.title: Specificity Beginner
docs.text:
Specificity is a score of three numbers: (IDs, classes, types). Compare left to right; the first higher number wins. 1,0,0 beats 0,15,0.

Selector Score Why * 0,0,0 Universal adds nothing li 0,0,1 1 type ul li 0,0,2 2 types .nav 0,1,0 1 class a:hover 0,1,1 pseudo-class counts as a class [type="email"] 0,1,0 attribute counts as a class li::before 0,0,2 pseudo-element counts as a type #main .nav a 1,1,1 :is(#a, .b) p 1,0,1 :is() takes its most specific argument :where(#a, .b) p 0,0,1 :where() is always 0 :not(.x) 0,1,0 takes its argument's specificity style="…" beats all selectors !important jumps to a higher origin Use only to override third-party CSS or in utilities

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

Keep specificity low and flat: mostly single classes. Use :where() in resets and libraries so users can override them with a single class. Use @layer instead of specificity hacks to manage order between reset, base, components and utilities. See Modern CSS → @layer.

docs.title: Inheritance Beginner
docs.text:
Some properties pass down from parent to children: mostly text properties (color, font-*, line-height, letter-spacing, text-align, visibility, cursor, list-style). Box properties (margin, padding, border, background, width, display) do not.

.parent { color: purple; border: 2px solid purple; }
/* Children are purple text, but get no border. */
Parent

Child: purple text inherited, no border

Control inheritance with these keywords, which work on any property:

Keyword Means inherit Use the parent's value initial Use the spec's initial value (display: initial is inline!) unset inherit if the property inherits, otherwise initial revert Go back to the browser's default style revert-layer Go back to the value from the previous cascade layer

docs.title: The box model Beginner
docs.text:
Every element is a rectangular box made of four layers:

margin border padding contentwidth × height 
.box {
  width: 200px;
  padding: 20px;
  border: 5px solid;
  margin: 10px;
}
box-sizing Total visible width content-box (default) 200 + 20×2 + 5×2 = 250px width = content only border-box 200px width includes padding + border

That's why every modern reset sets *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }.

<div class="cb">content-box</div>
<div class="bb">border-box</div>

.cb, .bb { width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid; }
.cb { box-sizing: content-box; }
.bb { box-sizing: border-box; }
content-box (250px) border-box (200px)

docs.title: Shorthand order Beginner
docs.text:
margin: 10px;                 /* all four */
margin: 10px 20px;            /* block (top/bottom) | inline (left/right) */
margin: 10px 20px 30px;       /* top | inline | bottom */
margin: 10px 20px 30px 40px;  /* top | right | bottom | left: clockwise */
margin-inline: auto;          /* centre a block with a width */

docs.title: display Beginner
display: none vs visibility: hidden vs opacity: 0
Margin collapse Intermediate
docs.text:
Vertical margins between block elements in normal flow merge into the larger of the two. They don't add up.

h2 { margin-bottom: 30px; }
p  { margin-top: 20px; }
/* Gap between them = 30px, not 50px */

Margins don't collapse inside flex or grid containers, or across a parent with padding, a border, or display: flow-root. A common surprise: a child's top margin "leaking" out of its parent. Fix it with display: flow-root on the parent, or use gap instead of margins.

Senior note · 🟡 Intermediate

Many teams avoid margin collapse entirely by using one direction only (margin-block-end) or, better, layout gap and the "stack" pattern: .stack > * + * { margin-block-start: var(--space, 1rem); }.

docs.title: Logical properties Intermediate
docs.text:
Logical properties follow the writing direction, so layouts flip automatically for right-to-left languages and vertical writing modes.

Physical Logical width / height inline-size / block-size margin-left / margin-right margin-inline-start / margin-inline-end margin-top / margin-bottom margin-block-start / margin-block-end padding-left + padding-right padding-inline top / bottom / left / right inset-block-start / … / inset-inline-end text-align: left text-align: start border-top-left-radius border-start-start-radius

docs.title: Formatting contexts Expert
docs.text: A block formatting context (BFC) is an isolated layout region: floats inside it are contained, and its children's margins don't collapse with outside margins. These create one: the root element, floats, absolutely positioned elements, display: flow-root, inline-block, table cells, overflow other than visible/clip, flex and grid items, contain: layout | content | paint, and multi-column containers. Knowing this explains most "why does my margin/float behave differently in here?" bugs.

docs.title: Modern CSS (2023–2026)
docs.text:
Features that changed how professional CSS is written. Each section gives the Baseline status and a fallback.

Feature Status (Oct 2026) Replaces Nesting Baseline 2023 Sass nesting :has() Baseline 2023 JS "add class to parent" code Container queries (size) Baseline 2023 JS ResizeObserver hacks, many media queries @layer Baseline 2022 Specificity wars, !important Subgrid Baseline 2023 Fixed heights to align card internals @scope Baseline 2025 BEM naming, CSS Modules (partly) @property Baseline 2024 — (enables animating variables) light-dark(), relative colours, color-mix() Baseline 2023–24 Sass colour functions Popover API, @starting-style Baseline 2024 JS menu/tooltip libraries View transitions (same-document) Baseline 2025 Animation libraries for state changes Anchor positioning Chromium 125+, Safari 26, Firefox in progress Popper.js / Floating UI Scroll-driven animations Chromium 115+, Safari 26 Scroll listeners, IntersectionObserver Container style queries Chromium 111+, Safari 18 Modifier classes field-sizing: content Chromium 123+ Auto-grow textarea JS interpolate-size / calc-size() Chromium 129+ JS height animations if(), custom functions (@function) Chromium 137+ (experimental elsewhere) Preprocessor logic

docs.title: @layer (cascade layers) Advanced
docs.text:
Layers let you control the cascade by intent instead of specificity. Later layers win over earlier layers, regardless of specificity.

/* 1. Declare the order once, at the very top */
@layer reset, base, vendor, components, utilities;

@layer reset {
  * { margin: 0; box-sizing: border-box; }
}
@layer base {
  a { color: royalblue; }
}
@layer vendor {
  @import url("datepicker.css") layer(vendor);   /* or import straight into a layer */
}
@layer components {
  .card a { color: inherit; }
}
@layer utilities {
  .text-red { color: crimson; }   /* single class, but beats .card a (0,1,1) because the layer is later */
}

/* Unlayered styles beat ALL layers */

<div class="card"><a class="text-red" href="#">Which colour?</a></div>
I'm crimson: the utilities layer wins over a more specific selector

Senior note · 🔴 Expert

@layer is the cleanest answer to "how do we integrate Tailwind, a component library and our own CSS without !important?" Put third-party CSS in a low layer, your components above it, utilities on top. Note the twist: for !important declarations the layer order is reversed, so an !important in reset beats an !important in utilities. That's deliberate: it lets low layers protect critical rules.

docs.title: Container queries Advanced
docs.text:
Media queries ask "how wide is the viewport?" Container queries ask "how wide is my container?" So a card can be stacked in a narrow sidebar and side-by-side in a wide main column, on the same screen.

.card-wrap { container-type: inline-size; container-name: card; }

.card { display: grid; gap: 1rem; }

@container card (width > 400px) {
  .card { grid-template-columns: 120px 1fr; }
}

Drag the bottom-right corner of the box to resize the container:

Container query cardNarrow container: stacked. Wider than 400px: side by side. Resize me ↘

Style queries (Chromium, Safari 18): query a custom property value on the container.

@container style(--variant: featured) {
  .card { border: 2px solid gold; }
}

docs.title: :has() Advanced
docs.text:
Covered in depth in Selectors. A few modern patterns:

/* Lock page scroll while a modal is open */
html:has(dialog[open]) { overflow: hidden; }

/* Form-level error state */
form:has(:user-invalid) .submit-hint { display: block; }

/* Layout switches on content */
.grid:has(> :nth-child(5)) { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); }

docs.title: Subgrid Advanced
docs.text:
Let a grid item's children line up with the parent's grid tracks. Perfect for card rows where titles, text and buttons should align across cards.

.cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 1rem; }
.card {
  display: grid;
  grid-row: span 3;                /* card occupies 3 row tracks of the parent */
  grid-template-rows: subgrid;     /* its children use those tracks */
}
Short title

One line.

Buy A much longer title that wraps onto two lines

Some text that is a bit longer than the others, so it takes up more space.

Buy Medium title

Two short lines of text here.

Buy

All titles, texts and buttons line up across cards, even though their content lengths differ.

docs.title: @scope Advanced Baseline 2025
docs.text:
Limit styles to a DOM subtree, with an optional lower boundary ("donut scope").

@scope (.card) to (.card__content) {
  img { border-radius: 8px; }   /* images in .card, but NOT inside .card__content */
  :scope { padding: 1rem; }     /* :scope = the .card itself */
}

Also gives proximity: when two scopes' rules have equal specificity, the closer scope root wins. Useful for nested light/dark themes.

docs.title: Anchor positioning Advanced Chromium 125+, Safari 26
docs.text:
Tether a positioned element (tooltip, menu) to another element, with automatic flipping when it hits the viewport edge. Replaces Popper.js / Floating UI for most cases.

<button popovertarget="tip" class="anchor">Hover target</button>
<div id="tip" popover>Anchored tooltip</div>

.anchor { anchor-name: --btn; }
#tip {
  position-anchor: --btn;
  position-area: top;                  /* place above the anchor */
  margin: 0 0 8px;
  position-try-fallbacks: flip-block;  /* flip below if there's no room above */
}
Click me Anchored to the button ✨

In a browser without anchor positioning, the popover falls back to the centre of the screen: still usable.

docs.title: Feature queries with @supports Intermediate
docs.text:
Progressive enhancement: write the baseline, then upgrade where supported.

.cards { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; }              /* works everywhere */

@supports (grid-template-rows: subgrid) {
  .cards { display: grid; /* … subgrid version … */ }
}

@supports selector(:has(a)) {
  .card:has(img) { /* … */ }
}

@supports not (anchor-name: --a) {
  .tooltip { /* JS-positioned fallback */ }
}

docs.title: Other modern features worth knowing Advanced
position Beginner
Offsets with inset Beginner
docs.text:
.overlay { position: absolute; inset: 0; }          /* top:0; right:0; bottom:0; left:0 */
.corner  { position: absolute; inset: auto 1rem 1rem auto; }   /* bottom-right */
.bar     { position: fixed; inset-inline: 0; inset-block-end: 0; }  /* full-width bottom bar */

docs.title: sticky Intermediate
docs.text:
.section-title { position: sticky; top: 0; background: white; }

Scroll inside the box:

A — sticky

Apple

Apricot

Avocado

B — sticky

Banana

Blackberry

Blueberry

C — sticky

Cherry

Coconut

Cranberry

Why isn't my sticky sticking?

  1. You forgot an offset (top: 0).
  2. An ancestor has overflow: hidden | auto | scroll. Sticky sticks within the nearest scrolling ancestor. Use overflow: clip if you just need clipping.
  3. The parent is exactly as tall as the sticky element, so there's no room to stick.
  4. In a flex/grid container, the item is stretched to full height. Add align-self: start.

docs.title: z-index and stacking contexts Intermediate → Advanced
docs.text:
z-index controls which overlapping element is on top. It applies to positioned elements and to flex/grid items.

The catch: z-index only competes within the same stacking context. A child with z-index: 9999 can never escape a parent whose stacking context is below a sibling.

<div class="a" style="position:relative; z-index:1">
  A (z 1)
  <div style="position:absolute; z-index:9999">child of A (z 9999)</div>
</div>
<div class="b" style="position:relative; z-index:2">B (z 2): on top of A's child!</div>
A (z-index 1) child of A (9999) B (z-index 2): still on top of A's child

What creates a stacking context:

  • The root <html>
  • position: absolute | relative with a z-index other than auto
  • position: fixed | sticky (always)
  • Flex/grid items with a z-index
  • opacity < 1
  • transform, scale, rotate, translate, filter, backdrop-filter, perspective, clip-path, mask (any non-none value)
  • mix-blend-mode other than normal
  • isolation: isolate (the clean, intentional way)
  • contain: layout | paint, container-type: size | inline-size
  • will-change naming any of the above
  • Top-layer elements (dialog, popovers, fullscreen) sit above everything, no z-index needed

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

Define a z-index scale as tokens (--z-dropdown: 100; --z-sticky: 200; --z-modal: 300; --z-toast: 400) and use isolation: isolate on components to contain their internal z-indexes. Better yet, move modals, menus and toasts to the top layer with <dialog> and popover; then z-index wars mostly disappear.

docs.title: overflow Beginner
docs.text:
overflow: visible;   /* default: content spills out */
overflow: hidden;    /* clip, still programmatically scrollable; creates a scroll container */

Floats were built for wrapping text around images. For about a decade they were also abused for page layouts. Today use them only for text wrap.

docs.title: :has(), the "parent selector" Advanced Baseline 2023
docs.text:
:has() selects an element based on what's inside it or after it. It replaces a huge amount of JavaScript "add a class to the parent" code.

/* A card that contains an image gets a different layout */
.card:has(img) { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 80px 1fr; }

/* A form field whose input is invalid gets a red label */
.field:has(input:user-invalid) label { color: crimson; }

/* Highlight the h2 that's directly followed by a p */
h2:has(+ p) { margin-bottom: 0; }

/* Dark mode toggle with no JS */
:root:has(#dark:checked) { color-scheme: dark; }

/* Dim siblings of the hovered card */
.grid:has(.card:hover) .card:not(:hover) { opacity: .5; }
Card with an image → becomes a grid Card without an image → stays a block Hover any card: the others dim

docs.title: Nesting Intermediate Baseline 2023
docs.text:
Native CSS nesting works like Sass nesting:

.card {
  padding: 1rem;

  & h3 { margin: 0; }          /* .card h3 */
  &:hover { box-shadow: 0 4px 12px #0002; }   /* .card:hover */
  &.featured { border: 2px solid gold; }      /* .card.featured */
  .theme-dark & { background: #222; }         /* .theme-dark .card */

  @media (width >= 600px) { padding: 2rem; }  /* media query inside */
}

The & is optional before a nested type selector in current browsers (h3 { } works), but keep it for clarity and older-browser safety.

docs.title: Selector performance Expert
docs.text: Browsers match selectors right to left: for .nav li a, they find every a, then check if it's inside an li, inside .nav. In practice, selector matching is rarely a bottleneck on modern engines. What actually costs time is style invalidation: a change that forces re-matching for many elements, such as toggling a class on <body> that a large :has() selector depends on. Keep :has() arguments narrow (.card:has(> img) rather than body:has(.x)), and use the DevTools Performance panel's "Selector stats" to find the expensive ones.

docs.title: HTML5: How It Works
docs.text:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes what content is: a heading, a paragraph, a button, a navigation menu. CSS then describes how it looks, and JavaScript describes how it behaves.

What “HTML5” means today

"HTML5" was the 2014 W3C snapshot. Since 2019 there's one HTML standard, the HTML Living Standard maintained by WHATWG, and it changes continuously. When people say HTML5 today, they mean "modern HTML". This playbook follows the Living Standard as of 2026.

docs.title: Elements, tags and attributes Beginner
docs.text:
<a href="https://example.com" target="_blank">Visit example</a>
Part In the example Meaning Opening tag <a …> Starts the element Attribute href="https://example.com" Extra information: name + value Content Visit example What's inside Closing tag </a> Ends the element Element the whole thing Opening tag + content + closing tag Visit example

Void elements have no content and no closing tag: <br>, <hr>, <img>, <input>, <meta>, <link>, <source>, <track>, <wbr>, <area>, <base>, <col>, <embed>. Writing <br/> with a slash is allowed but has no effect in HTML.

Boolean attributes are on when present and off when absent: <input disabled>. Writing disabled="false" still disables it.

docs.title: Block vs inline Beginner
docs.text:
By default, each element has a CSS display value.

  • Block elements (<div>, <p>, <h1>, <section>, <ul>) start on a new line and stretch to fill the width.
  • Inline elements (<span>, <a>, <strong>, <em>, <code>) sit inside a line of text and are only as wide as their content.
<div style="background:#ffd8c2">I'm a block div</div>
<div style="background:#c7e2ff">So am I, on a new line</div>
<span style="background:#ffd8c2">I'm inline</span>
<span style="background:#c7e2ff">I sit on the same line</span>
I'm a block div So am I, on a new line I'm inline I sit on the same line

Senior note · 🟡 Intermediate

"Block" and "inline" are CSS behaviours, not HTML rules. The HTML spec uses content categories instead: flow, phrasing, heading, sectioning, embedded, interactive, metadata. These decide what can be nested inside what. For example, <p> accepts only phrasing content, so <p><div>…</div></p> is invalid; the browser closes the <p> before the <div>.

Rule of thumb: interactive content can't be nested inside interactive content. A <button> inside an <a> is invalid and confuses screen readers and keyboards.

<!-- ❌ Div soup -->
<div class="header"><div class="nav">…</div></div>
<div class="button" onclick="save()">Save</div>

<!-- ✅ Semantic -->
<header><nav>…</nav></header>
<button type="button" onclick="save()">Save</button>

The semantic version gives you, for free:

  • Keyboard support: <button> is focusable and responds to Enter and Space.
  • Screen reader support: announced as "Save, button"; landmarks let users jump to the nav.
  • SEO: search engines understand page structure.
  • Less code: no tabindex, role or key handlers to write and maintain.
